title: The River That Changed Course
summary: A village elder tells two children the true story of how the river near their village shifted its path after a long-ago flood, and the children investigate the old riverbed together.
poll: Old stories told by elders are just as useful as physical evidence for understanding the past.

versions.title: The River That Changed Course
versions.text:
Nour and Zaid live by a river. It is next to their small village. Their grandfather is Saad. Saad is an elder in the village.

One night, Saad tells them a story. Long ago, a flood came. Rain fell for many days. The river grew big and strong.

The flood pushed through the land. It swept rocks and mud. Near a hill, it cut a new path. The old path went dry.

Nour and Zaid want to see it. The next day, they walk there.

The old path is dry now. Smooth stones cover the ground. Old trees stand in a line. They mark the dry channel.

Then the kids look at the new river. It flows near the hill now.

Saad tells them why. Water flows down. It takes the easy path. The flood gave it more force. So the river made a new path.

Now Nour and Zaid know the tale. The dry path and the new river tell it together.

The flood pushed through the land. It carried rocks, sand, and mud. Near a hill, it cut a new path. The old path slowly went dry.

Nour and Zaid want to see this. The next day, they walk to the old riverbed.

Then the kids walk to the river today. It flows near the hill. It takes a new, easier path.

That night, Saad tells them why. Water always flows downhill. It picks the path that is easiest. The flood gave it extra force. So the water cut a new path. It never went back.

Now Nour and Zaid know the tale. The dry old path and the new river tell one story.

Nour and Zaid live by a quiet river, next to their small village. Their grandpa, Saad, is a wise elder. He remembers many old tales from long ago.

One night, Saad tells the children a story about the river. Long ago, he says, a huge flood changed the land. Heavy rain fell for many days. It did not stop. The river grew wide, fast, and very strong.

The rushing flood carried rocks, sand, and thick mud down the valley. Near a hill, it cut a brand-new path. The ground there was soft. The river's old path slowly became dry.

Nour and Zaid are curious. They want to see this old path for themselves. The next morning, they walk together to the old riverbed.

The old channel is dry and silent now. Smooth stones cover the ground. Moving water polished them over many years. A line of old trees still grows along the dry path. It marks where the river used to flow long ago.

Next, the children walk to the river that flows today. It curves around the hill now. It takes a new, easier path.

That night, Saad explains why rivers change course. Flowing water always moves downhill. It picks the easiest path it can find. The flood gave the water extra force. So it carved a new path. The river never went back to its old channel.

Now Nour and Zaid understand the river's story. The dry old riverbed and the new river, together, tell the story of that long-ago flood.

One evening, Saad tells the children an old story about the river near their home. Long ago, he explains, a tremendous flood completely reshaped the terrain around the village, permanently altering its course and surprising everyone who lived there at the time, since nothing in living memory had prepared them for it.

Heavy rain fell for many days without stopping, filling the whole valley with rushing runoff. In valleys like this one, rare but intense storms can send enormous amounts of water downhill very quickly, overwhelming whatever channel the water normally follows. The river grew wide, fast, and extremely powerful, and the rushing current carried heavy boulders, sand, and thick sediment down the valley floor, depositing much of it wherever the current slowed enough to drop its load. Near a hill, the flood's force cut a brand-new channel through the soft ground, while the river's old path slowly dried up and was abandoned completely. Saad says people still remember that particular year, because the water rose almost to the edge of the village and families had to move their animals to higher ground until the current finally slowed down.

Nour and Zaid are curious about this old story, so the next morning they walk together to the old riverbed to investigate what remains of it with their own eyes.

The old channel is dry and silent now, half hidden among scattered boulders and layers of deposit left behind by the retreating water. Smooth stones cover the ground, worn down by years of erosion as moving water rubbed against them again and again, generation after generation. A line of old trees still grows along the curve of the dry path, marking exactly where the river used to meander long ago, their roots reaching deep underground in search of any remaining moisture.

Next, the children walk to where the river flows today. It meanders around the base of the hill, following a new, gentler gradient down toward the fields below, where farmers now rely on the water to grow their crops. A visiting geologist once told the village that this gentler gradient explains why the flood water preferred the new route over the old one, since water naturally finds the terrain that costs it the least energy.

That evening, Saad explains carefully why rivers sometimes change their course entirely. Flowing water always moves downhill, and it naturally follows whichever path requires the least effort to travel. During the great flood, there was so much extra force in the rushing water that it was able to carve a brand-new channel around the hill, and once it had done so, the river never returned to its old bed again.

By the end of the evening, Nour and Zaid understand the river's whole story. The dry old riverbed and the new river, taken together, tell the story of that long-ago flood — a story that their grandfather's memory and their own careful investigating both helped to explain fully.

keyWords.definition: a lot of water that covers land that is normally dry
keyWords.example: The flood covered the field with water after the storm.

keyWords.definition: an older person who is respected for their experience and knowledge
keyWords.example: The village elder told stories about the old days.

keyWords.definition: the path a river follows as it flows
keyWords.example: The boat floated down the narrow channel.
The dry riverbed had no water in it at all.

keyWords.definition: the way something, like water, moves from one place to another
keyWords.example: The ball rolled down a straight path.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Two children who build a new house beside a quiet river with their father and mother
A flood that made a river change its path, and two children who investigate it
A village that has no water at all in the summer months, so people must walk far
A trip to buy new stones for a garden at the old school with a teacher and some friends
questions.why: The story tells how a long-ago flood changed the river's path, and how Nour and Zaid explore the old riverbed to understand it.

wrong.A: The story is not about building a house.
wrong.C: The village has a river; it is not without water.
wrong.D: The story does not mention buying stones.

questions.stem: Why did the river's old path become dry?
options: A flood cut a new path around a hill
The villagers filled it in with sand
The sun dried it up in one day
Saad built a wall across it
questions.why: The story says the flood cut a brand-new path near the hill, so the old path slowly became dry.

wrong.B: The villagers did not fill in the path.
wrong.C: The path dried up over time, not in one day.
wrong.D: Saad did not build a wall.

questions.stem: What do Nour and Zaid find at the old riverbed?
options: A new bridge made of wood and rope
Smooth stones and a line of old trees
A pile of fresh mud near the water
Fish swimming in the water of the pond
questions.why: The story says smooth stones cover the ground, and a line of old trees grows along the dry path.

wrong.A: There is no bridge mentioned.
wrong.C: The riverbed is dry, with old stones, not fresh mud.
wrong.D: There is no water there now, so no fish.

questions.stem: In the story, a channel is —
options: a kind of smooth stone
the path a river follows
a type of old tree
a village elder's name
questions.why: The story uses channel to mean the path that the river's water follows.

wrong.A: A channel is not a stone.
wrong.C: A channel is not a tree.
wrong.D: Saad is the elder's name, not a channel.

questions.stem: Who tells Nour and Zaid the story about the flood?
options: Their teacher
A stranger from another village
Their grandfather, Saad
A book they found
questions.why: The story says their grandfather, Saad, an elder in the village, tells them the story one evening.

wrong.A: No teacher is mentioned.
wrong.B: The storyteller is their grandfather, not a stranger.
wrong.D: They hear the story from Saad, not from a book.

questions.stem: Why does the river always flow along the easiest path downhill?
options: Because villagers dig the path for it every year with big tools and shovels
Because flowing water naturally moves toward the path that takes the least effort
Because the old trees pull the water toward them with their strong roots
Because the stones push the water uphill as it flows along the ground
questions.why: Saad explains that water always moves downhill and picks whichever path is easiest, which is why the flood could cut a new one.

wrong.A: No one digs a path for the river.
wrong.C: Trees do not pull water.
wrong.D: Water does not move uphill.

questions.stem: What can you tell from the smooth stones in the old riverbed?
options: Someone carved them by hand
Water used to flow over them for a long time
They fell from the hill recently
They were always smooth, even before the flood
questions.why: Moving water polishes stones smooth over time, so the smooth stones show that water flowed there for a long time in the past.

wrong.A: The story does not say anyone carved the stones.
wrong.C: The stones are old, not recent.
wrong.D: The flowing water is what made them smooth.

questions.stem: Why do the children walk to both the old riverbed and the new river?
options: To compare the two paths and understand how the river changed
To fish in both places with a net and a line, for food and for fun
To plant new trees along both paths by the river with a spade
To ask the river for permission to visit its banks in the spring
questions.why: Looking at both the dry old path and the flowing new path helps Nour and Zaid understand how and why the river changed course.

wrong.B: There is no fishing in the story.
wrong.C: The children do not plant trees.
wrong.D: Rivers cannot give permission.

LOW.prompt: Would you rather learn about the flood from Saad's story or from walking to the old riverbed yourself? Explain your answer using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said which way I would choose.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I would want to walk to the old riverbed myself, like Nour and Zaid did. I could see the smooth stones that the water polished long ago. I could also see the line of old trees that still grows along the dry path. Listening to Saad's story would be nice too, but seeing the proof with my own eyes would help me understand it best.

keyWords.definition: the slow wearing away of rock or soil by water, wind, or ice
keyWords.example: Years of erosion carved a deep groove into the cliff.

keyWords.definition: a surface that is higher on one end than the other, like a hillside
keyWords.example: The ball rolled quickly down the steep slope.

keyWords.definition: a very large rock, usually rounded by weather or water
keyWords.example: A huge boulder blocked the narrow mountain trail.

keyWords.definition: small pieces of rock, sand, or soil carried and left behind by moving water
keyWords.example: A layer of sediment settled at the bottom of the pond.

keyWords.definition: to look closely at something in order to find out more about it
keyWords.example: The students went outside to investigate the strange footprints.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: Nour and Zaid spend their weekend building a brand-new bridge across the wide river.
A long-ago flood reshaped the river's course, and the children investigate to learn why.
Saad spends an entire afternoon teaching the two children how to swim across the river.
The village elder angrily refuses to tell the curious children any stories about the past.
questions.why: The story centers on the flood that reshaped the river's course and the children's investigation of the old riverbed and the new river.

wrong.A: No bridge is built in the story.
wrong.C: Saad tells a story; he does not teach swimming.
wrong.D: Saad happily shares the story with the children.

questions.stem: What carried the heavy boulders and sediment down the valley during the flood?
options: The villagers' carts and mules
A group of travelers on camels
The rushing flood current
A herd of animals from the hills
questions.why: The story says the rushing current carried heavy boulders, sand, and thick sediment down through the valley.

wrong.A: Carts are not mentioned.
wrong.B: No travelers are mentioned carrying material.
wrong.D: Animals did not carry the boulders and sediment.

questions.stem: According to the story, where did families move their animals during the flood?
options: Across the river to another village
Into their homes
To higher ground
Onto the old, dry riverbed
questions.why: Saad says the water rose almost to the edge of the village, so families moved their animals to higher ground.

wrong.A: The story does not mention crossing to another village.
wrong.B: Homes would not keep animals safe from rising water.
wrong.D: The old riverbed is where the water came from before; moving there would not be safer.

questions.stem: What does erosion mean in this story?
options: A sudden, powerful flood that fills the valley in an hour
The slow wearing away of stone by moving water over time
A new path cut in one single day by the villagers
A grandfather telling an old story to the children
questions.why: The story describes stones worn down by years of erosion as water rubbed against them again and again.

wrong.A: A flood is a separate idea from erosion itself.
wrong.C: Erosion happens slowly over years, not in one day.
wrong.D: Erosion is a process, not a person telling a story.

questions.stem: Why did the river choose the new, gentler slope instead of returning to its old channel?
options: Because flowing water naturally follows the path that takes the least effort
Because villagers blocked the old channel on purpose with big stones and heavy logs last year
Because the old trees grew across the old path and stopped the flow, years and years ago
Because the new slope has more boulders and rocks to flow around, so the water likes it better
questions.why: Saad explains that water always moves downhill along whichever path requires the least effort, which is why it kept the new, gentler route.

wrong.B: The story does not say villagers blocked anything.
wrong.C: The trees grow along the old path; they did not block it.
wrong.D: More boulders would not make a path easier to follow.

questions.stem: What can you infer about the smooth stones and layers of sediment left in the old channel?
options: They prove that moving water once flowed there for a long time
They were placed there recently by local farmers who moved them
They show that the channel was always completely dry and empty
They have nothing at all to do with the long-ago flood
questions.why: Smooth stones and sediment layers are physical evidence left by moving water, showing that water once flowed and later deposited material there.

wrong.B: The story does not say farmers placed these there.
wrong.C: If the channel were always dry, water could not have shaped the stones.
wrong.D: These are direct evidence of the flood described in the story.

questions.stem: Why does the river's old path slowly dry up instead of drying up all at once?
options: Because the flood itself happened very gradually over many long years
Because less water flowed there once the river found an easier path
Because the villagers slowly and carefully dug up the old channel
Because the sun's heat slowly increased little by little each single year
questions.why: Once the river found its new, easier path, water stopped flowing through the old channel, so it gradually dried out.

wrong.A: The flood itself happened over days, not years.
wrong.C: No digging by villagers is mentioned.
wrong.D: The sun's heat is not given as the reason in the story.

questions.stem: How does the author organize this story?
options: By comparing two different rivers in two different countries, then telling how the children visit each one of them
By telling Saad's story of the flood, then following the children as they investigate and Saad explains why it happened
By listing the exact dates of every flood in the village's history, one by one, from the oldest flood to the newest one
By describing how to build a boat to cross the new river, with each tool and each step that is needed
questions.why: The story moves from Saad's telling of the flood, to the children's investigation of the old and new paths, to Saad's explanation of why rivers change course.

wrong.A: Only one river and one village are described.
wrong.C: No exact dates are listed.
wrong.D: The story does not explain how to build a boat.

MID.prompt: Explain how Nour and Zaid used both Saad's story and their own investigation to understand why the river changed course. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how the story and the investigation worked together.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Nour and Zaid learned about the flood in two different ways. First, Saad told them that heavy rain fell for days and the flood carried boulders and sediment that cut a new channel near the hill. Then the children investigated the old riverbed themselves, where they found smooth stones shaped by erosion and a line of old trees marking the old path. By combining Saad's story with their own careful investigating, they understood both what happened and why the river never returned to its old slope.

keyWords.definition: to follow a winding, curving path instead of a straight one, especially describing a river
keyWords.example: The stream meanders slowly through the wide, flat valley.

keyWords.definition: the natural features of an area of land, such as its shape and surface
keyWords.example: The hikers studied the rocky terrain before planning their route.

keyWords.definition: material, such as sand or mud, that has been left behind by moving water, wind, or ice
keyWords.example: A thick deposit of sand covered the old riverbank.

keyWords.definition: the steepness or slope of a surface, such as the ground a river flows over
keyWords.example: The road's steep gradient made the bike ride difficult.

keyWords.definition: a scientist who studies rocks, soil, and the history of the Earth's surface
keyWords.example: The geologist examined the layers of rock in the cliff.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: A village elder's memory alone fully explains every detail of how the river's course changed, and no other evidence of any kind is needed.
A long-ago flood permanently altered the river's course, and oral memory together with physical evidence in the terrain explain how and why.
Rivers never change course once they have been established in a particular channel, so the story is a legend only.
A visiting geologist discovered the old riverbed before any villager knew it existed, and the elder had no part in the story.
questions.why: The story shows that Saad's memory and the children's investigation of the terrain, boulders, and deposits together explain the river's permanent change of course.

wrong.A: The children's own investigation adds evidence beyond Saad's memory alone.
wrong.C: The story's whole point is that this river's course did change.
wrong.D: Villagers already knew the old riverbed existed before any geologist visited.

questions.stem: What happened to the heavy boulders and sediment the flood carried once the current slowed down?
options: They washed all the way out to the distant sea
They were carried back upstream to the village
They were deposited in layers wherever the current lost speed
They dissolved completely and disappeared in the floodwater
questions.why: The story explains that the rushing current deposited much of the material it carried wherever it slowed down enough to drop its load.

wrong.A: The story never mentions the material reaching a sea.
wrong.B: Moving water does not carry sediment back upstream.
wrong.D: Rock and sediment do not dissolve in water.

questions.stem: According to the visiting geologist, why did the floodwater prefer the new route around the hill?
options: The new route had a gentler gradient that cost less energy
The old channel had been deliberately blocked by the villagers
The new route was considerably shorter in total distance
The hill itself physically moved a little during the flood
questions.why: The geologist explained that the gentler gradient of the new route required less energy for the flowing water to follow, which is why it became the river's permanent path.

wrong.B: No blocking by villagers is mentioned.
wrong.C: Distance is not what the geologist discusses.
wrong.D: Hills do not move during a flood.

questions.stem: In the story, the word meander means —
options: to flow in a straight, direct line toward the sea
to dry up completely and disappear within a single day
to carry heavy boulders and sediment far downstream
to follow a winding, curving path instead of a straight one
questions.why: The story describes the river as meandering around the base of the hill, meaning it follows a curving rather than a straight path.

wrong.A: Meandering describes curving movement, the opposite of a straight line.
wrong.B: Meander describes flowing, not drying up.
wrong.C: Carrying boulders is a separate detail, not what meander means.

questions.stem: Based on the story, why do the old trees along the dry channel still grow there today?
options: Villagers water them by hand every week, carrying jars from the well in the village
Their roots reach deep underground toward moisture that remains from the old channel
They were planted recently to mark the new river's path across the dry valley floor
They do not actually need any water to survive, because desert trees live on sunlight alone
questions.why: The story explains that the old trees' roots reach deep underground in search of remaining moisture, which is why they continue growing along the now-dry channel.

wrong.A: No hand-watering is mentioned.
wrong.C: The trees mark the old path, not the new river.
wrong.D: All plants need some water; these trees find it underground.

questions.stem: Put these events in the order they happened.
options: Nour and Zaid investigate the old riverbed, heavy rain falls, the flood cuts a new channel
The flood cuts a new channel, heavy rain falls, Saad tells his story to the children
Heavy rain falls, the flood cuts a new channel, Nour and Zaid investigate the old riverbed
Saad tells his story to the children, the flood cuts a new channel, heavy rain falls
questions.why: First the heavy rain fell, then the flood's force cut the new channel, and only afterward, long after, do Nour and Zaid investigate the old riverbed.

wrong.A: The children's investigation happens long after the flood, not before it.
wrong.B: The rain had to fall before the flood could cut a new channel.
wrong.D: Saad's story is told long after the flood, not before it.

questions.stem: What can readers infer from the layers of deposit found in the old channel?
options: They show exactly which year the great flood occurred in the valley, and the name of the river
They provide physical evidence that confirms the moving water carried and dropped material there over time
They prove that the old channel was never actually part of the river at all, only a road
They were placed there by the geologist during a recent visit to the site, to confuse the students
questions.why: Deposits of sediment are physical evidence left behind by moving water, supporting Saad's account that the flood's current once flowed through that channel.

wrong.A: The deposits do not give an exact date.
wrong.C: The deposits show the channel WAS part of the river's path, not the opposite.
wrong.D: The geologist studied the deposits; he did not create them.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the geologist's explanation about the gradient near the end of the story?
options: To argue that Saad's story cannot be trusted and that the children made it up
To connect the children's physical evidence with a scientific reason that supports Saad's account
To describe in detail how geologists collect rock samples from the dry riverbed
To suggest that the river will soon change course again and flood the village houses near the old well
questions.why: The geologist's explanation gives a scientific reason, the gentler gradient, that supports and strengthens both the physical evidence and Saad's remembered story.

wrong.A: The geologist's explanation supports Saad's story rather than questioning it.
wrong.C: The story does not describe sample-collecting methods.
wrong.D: The story does not suggest another change is coming.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says old stories told by elders are just as useful as physical evidence for understanding the past. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Saad's account and the children's investigation.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that old stories told by elders can be just as useful as physical evidence, when the two are used together. Saad's memory gave Nour and Zaid the full narrative: the heavy rain, the flood's force, and the new channel it carved around the hill. On its own, though, his story could not prove exactly how the land changed. That proof came from the terrain itself: the eroded boulders, the layers of deposit, and the gentler gradient the geologist identified. Someone might argue that physical evidence is more reliable because it cannot be misremembered, but Saad's story explained details, like the families moving their animals, that the terrain alone could never reveal. Together, memory and evidence told a fuller story than either could alone.

LOW.stem: What did the flood sweep along with it?
options: Rocks and mud
Boats and fish
Houses and cars
Trees and bridges
LOW.why: The text says the flood swept rocks and mud through the land.

wrong.B: Boats and fish are not mentioned.
wrong.C: The text does not say houses or cars were swept away.
wrong.D: The trees stand in a line by the old path; they were not swept away.

LOW.stem: Why did the flood cut a new path near the hill?
options: The ground was very hard.
Saad dug it with a tool.
The water had more force.
There was no rain at all.
LOW.why: The text says the flood gave the water more force, so the river made a new path.

wrong.A: The new path was cut by force, not made easy by hard ground.
wrong.B: Saad only tells the story; he did not dig.
wrong.D: Rain fell for many days.

LOW.stem: In the story, the word elder means —
options: a small child
an older wise man
a kind of river
a village road
LOW.why: Saad is the grandfather and an elder in the village who tells the story.

wrong.A: Saad is the children's grandfather, not a child.
wrong.C: An elder is a person, not water.
wrong.D: Saad is a person in the village, not a road.

LOW.stem: What do the old trees in a line show?
options: Where the village stops
Where the hill begins
Where the kids play
Where the old river ran
LOW.why: The text says the old trees stand in a line and mark the dry channel.

wrong.A: The trees mark the old channel, not the village edge.
wrong.B: The hill is by the new river path.
wrong.C: The trees are not about the children's games.

MID.stem: How long did the heavy rain fall before the flood?
options: One night
A few hours
Many days
A whole year
MID.why: The text says heavy rain fell for many days without stopping.

wrong.A: The rain fell for many days, not one night.
wrong.B: A few hours is far too short.
wrong.D: The text says many days, not a year.

MID.stem: What do the old trees along the dry path tell the children?
options: Where the river used to flow
Where the next flood will come
Where the farmers plant seeds
Where the village will grow
MID.why: The text says the line of old trees marks where the river used to flow.

wrong.B: The text does not predict any new flood.
wrong.C: Farmers are not mentioned near the trees.
wrong.D: The trees tell about the past river, not the village's future.

MID.stem: In the story, the word investigate means —
options: to forget something
to sleep nearby
to build a new path
to look closely
MID.why: The children walk to the old riverbed to see what remains and learn about the flood.

wrong.A: The children want to learn, not forget.
wrong.B: They walk there in the morning to look around.
wrong.C: The flood built the new path; the children did not.

MID.stem: How is the old channel different from the river today?
options: Both are dry and silent.
The old is dry; the new flows.
The old one is fast; the new is dry.
Both curve around the hill.
MID.why: The old channel is dry and silent now, while the river today flows around the hill.

wrong.A: The river today still carries water.
wrong.C: It is the old channel that is dry.
wrong.D: Only the new river curves around the hill.

HIGH.stem: How close did the floodwater rise to the village, according to Saad?
options: Almost to the edge of the village
Into every house in the village
Only as far as the hill
Just to the old trees
HIGH.why: The text says people remember that year because the water rose almost to the edge of the village.

wrong.B: The water rose almost to the edge, not into every house.
wrong.C: The text does not limit the water to the hill.
wrong.D: The trees line the old channel, not the water's highest point.

HIGH.stem: Why can rare but intense storms overwhelm a river's usual channel?
options: The river has no banks.
Water rushes down fast.
The villagers block the water.
The ground is always frozen.
HIGH.why: The text says enormous amounts of water move downhill so fast that the normal channel cannot hold it.

wrong.A: The text does not say the river has no banks.
wrong.C: The villagers do not block the water in the text.
wrong.D: Nothing says the ground is frozen; it is soft.

HIGH.stem: In the story, the word abandoned in "was abandoned" most nearly means —
options: cleaned carefully
filled with boats
left behind, not used
made wider and faster
HIGH.why: The old path dried up after the river moved, so the river left it behind.

wrong.A: The path dried up; no one cleaned it.
wrong.B: The old path is dry, so boats could not use it.
wrong.D: The new channel is where the river grew strong, not the old one.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author end by saying the dry riverbed and the new river "taken together" tell the story?
options: Both are near the village school.
Both are the same age as Saad.
Neither one has changed in years.
Each one shows the old flood.
HIGH.why: The dry old channel and the new river both show what the flood did to the land.

wrong.A: A school is never mentioned.
wrong.B: The text does not compare them to Saad's age.
wrong.C: Both are results of change caused by the flood.
